opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that a lot of it is genuinely impressive, and I don't want to be one of those people who just dismisses it. The fact that you can take a fairly simple architecture, train it on enormous amounts of data with stochastic gradient descent, and get systems that recognize objects in images, transcribe speech, translate between languages, and produce fluent, often quite coherent text: if you'd asked people in the field twenty years ago whether that would work, most of them would have said no. So there's a real empirical surprise there, and we should take it seriously.

What strikes me most is how much the representations learned in these networks seem to capture. In vision, for example, the intermediate layers end up encoding features that look a lot like what you'd find in the visual cortex: edges, textures, parts of objects. Nobody programmed that in. And with the large language models, they have absorbed an enormous amount of the regularity of human language, and with it some of the regularity of the world that language describes. That's remarkable.

That said, I think we have to be careful about what exactly we're impressed by. A lot of the performance comes from scale, from essentially having seen something close to the test case before, and when you probe them, you find they often haven't learned the underlying concept in a robust, generalizable way. We saw this with Go programs, for instance: superhuman by every standard measure, and yet amateur players could beat them with certain strategies, because the system had never really grasped what a group of stones is. It's a circuit, and circuits are not a very expressive representation for things like that. You need vast amounts of data to approximate concepts that could be written down compactly in a more expressive language.

So my view is: impressive engineering and a striking empirical finding, but I don't think it's the whole story of intelligence. I suspect we'll need to combine it with more structured, expressive representations — the kind of knowledge and reasoning that the field worked on for decades — to get systems that generalize the way humans do. And of course, the more capable these systems get, the more pressing the question of how we keep control over them becomes, which is the thing I care about most.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that they do things that, twenty or thirty years ago, most of us in AI would have said were a long way off. Take machine translation, or image recognition, or speech recognition. These were problems where decades of careful, hand-engineered approaches produced systems that worked, but not very well, and the deep learning systems simply blew past them. And they did it with a relatively simple recipe: lots of data, lots of compute, and gradient descent on a very large function approximator. There's a kind of brute elegance to that. The networks discover intermediate representations, features at various levels of abstraction, that nobody designed and that in some cases turn out to be quite sensible when you look at them.

And of course the large language models have taken that further. The fluency is genuinely remarkable. They can write a passable sonnet, summarize a legal document, answer questions about chemistry, all from the same underlying system. When I first used one, I had the same reaction most people did, which was a kind of astonishment.

But I'd want to be careful about what exactly we're impressed by. I'm impressed by the capability. I'm much less sure we understand why it works, or what's really going on inside. We don't have a good theory of these systems. We can't look at a trained network and say with confidence what it knows, what it believes, what goals it might be pursuing. And historically in AI, when we built something we didn't understand and it worked, that was a reason for caution rather than celebration. So I'd say I'm impressed, and I'm somewhat uneasy, and I think both of those reactions are appropriate.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a large function approximator and learned features at multiple abstraction levels, but does not state that complex functions of high-dimensional inputs require a hypothesis space that is both wide and deep.

astra-6.text:
What I find impressive is that we can take a fairly general learning architecture and, with enough data, get it to perform tasks that resisted decades of painstaking engineering. Image recognition and speech recognition are good examples. We used to spend enormous effort designing features, deciding what the system ought to look for. Now the system can learn useful representations for itself, and that’s a substantial achievement.

The interesting question is how far that takes us. Recognizing patterns very well doesn’t automatically give you the ability to reason, plan, or understand how the world works. So I’m impressed by the capabilities, while still thinking there are fundamental problems left to solve.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find impressive is that we can take a task where we really don’t know how to write down the solution—recognizing an object in an image, for example—and have a system learn to do it from examples. The ability to learn useful representations, rather than having people painstakingly design all the features, is a tremendous advance.

But I think we have to distinguish that achievement from the broader problem of intelligence. Getting very good at a particular task doesn’t necessarily mean that a system understands what it’s doing, or can take what it has learned and use it flexibly in a new situation. The results are impressive; the question is what ingredients are still missing.
